messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David joined the police force at eighteen, younger than almost anyone in his academy class, driven by a fierce, unspoken need to be the one who could stop things. He was sharp, physically capable, and had an intensity that his instructors mistook for pure focus. But six months into the job, that intensity had curdled into something else, a raw-edged vigilance that was beginning to fray. The reason he sought help began a decade earlier, in the suffocating quiet of his childhood living room. He remembers it not as a story but as a series of still photographs: his mother’s face, tight with fear; a half-empty glass on the coffee table; his father’s eyes, cold and distant. Then, a sudden, brutal movement as his father grabbed his mother’s arm. In those moments, David was frozen in an armchair across the room, his small body rigid, feeling as though he were trying to shrink into the cushions. When the memories come now, it is this physical reenactment he feels first—his own muscles locking, his posture curling inward as if to absorb a blow. An overwhelming, childish grief always follows, a sorrow for the boy who could do nothing but watch.

This history now dictates his present. Because he had come to believe, on a level deeper than words, that he can’t stop bad things from happening, David’s world is a landscape of imminent danger. This deeply ingrained sense of helplessness fuels a constant, exhausting threat assessment. He avoids unfamiliar sectors of the city on his patrol routes, convinced he won't be able to properly assess the danger and will be caught unprepared. He is the first to notice potential weapons in any room—a heavy ashtray in an interview suite, a letter opener on a desk during a routine call—cataloging them automatically. This perpetual state of high alert makes him exquisitely sensitive. Unusual silence, in particular, feels menacing, a held breath before an explosion, just like it was in his childhood home.

These interlocking beliefs and feelings have created a punishing cycle that dominates his life on the force. The fear that he is going crazy makes him even more reactive, so that an accidental brush from a colleague in the precinct feels less like an accident and more like a personal assault. Such moments of unexpected touch or intense discomfort act as immediate triggers. When a suspect on a street corner recently looked at him sideways, that suspicious glance was enough to plunge him back into the memory. He was no longer on a city street but back in that living room, seeing his father’s face in the suspect’s. The memories themselves have rewired his responses, making any unexpected touch feel like the start of that remembered violence.

The moment the images return, the present morphs into the past. In the middle of a routine traffic stop, his focus can suddenly shift from the driver to every potential weapon in the car, his mind convinced that violence is seconds away. This constant scanning for danger seems to prime his mind for the worst, making it easier for the old memories to surface. Recalling his own small body, frozen in the armchair, cements the conviction that he can’t rely on himself. The wave of grief that follows each time feels like proof of his fundamental helplessness. This belief that he is broken, in turn, makes the memories feel more powerful and intrusive, as if his own mind is an enemy he can’t control. Living in a state of constant threat assessment exhausts him, feeding the terrifying thought that his reactions mean he is losing his grip on reality.

The consequences have become undeniable. His partner has commented on his volatility, his tendency to escalate situations that don't warrant it. After a domestic disturbance call last month—one that was only a verbal argument—David couldn't shake the snapshot images for days, his body tight and his temper short with everyone. He came to therapy not because of a single event, but because of the suffocating accumulation of them. He feels he is failing at the one job he chose to prove he wasn't helpless. His greatest fear is no longer what others might do, but that his own mind is betraying him, and that soon, he won't be able to tell the difference between a memory and a real and present danger.
